readAloud.text: Three-dimensional printing has moved from industrial laboratories into everyday use. Engineers now print replacement parts for machines, doctors print models of organs for surgical planning, and architects create detailed building models within hours. The technology works by building an object layer by layer from a digital design, which reduces material waste considerably. As printers become cheaper and materials improve, many households are expected to own one within the next decade.

Sea turtles can migrate thousands of kilometres across open ocean and still return to the beach where they hatched. Researchers believe the animals detect the Earth's magnetic field and use it like an internal compass, storing a kind of magnetic map of their home coastline. Understanding this ability matters, because coastal development and artificial lighting can disorient hatchlings and disrupt entire populations.

Paper money first appeared in China during the Tang and Song dynasties, when merchants grew tired of carrying heavy strings of copper coins. Early banknotes were backed by deposits of precious metal, and governments gradually assumed the right to issue them. When Marco Polo described the system to European readers, many refused to believe that paper could hold real value, yet his account eventually influenced modern banking.

Dogs were the first animals ever domesticated, and the partnership began long before farming. Genetic evidence suggests that wolves started gathering around human camps to scavenge leftovers, and the tamest individuals gradually evolved into companions. Over thousands of years, selective breeding produced enormous variety, from tiny lapdogs to herding and hunting breeds, each shaped for a particular role in human society.

Early maps were often works of art as much as tools of navigation, decorated with sea monsters and imaginary lands. The great turning point came with Mercator's projection of 1569, which distorted the size of continents but preserved compass bearings as straight lines. Sailors could therefore plot a course with a ruler, and navigational maps have been shaped by that practical compromise ever since.

Deserts are defined not by heat but by dryness: any region receiving less than about 250 millimetres of rain a year qualifies. Many great deserts, including the Sahara, formed because mountain ranges force moist air to rise and shed its water long before it reaches the far side. This phenomenon, known as the rain shadow effect, explains why some of the driest places on Earth lie beside snow-capped peaks.

The first public film screenings in 1895 reportedly caused audiences to leap from their seats as a train appeared to rush towards them. Within two decades, silent cinema had become a global industry, and directors were already experimenting with close-ups, editing, and lighting to shape emotion. Sound arrived in the late 1920s, transforming the art form almost overnight and ending the careers of many silent stars.

retellLecture.title: How GPS works
retellLecture.sample: The lecture explained how GPS works. The speaker said that over twenty satellites orbit about twenty thousand kilometres above the Earth, each carrying a precise atomic clock and continuously broadcasting its position and the exact time. A ground receiver measures the travel time of each signal to calculate its distance, and signals from at least four satellites fix a position in three dimensions. The speaker also noted that without relativistic clock corrections, errors of kilometres would build up every day.
retellLecture.text: Satellite navigation has become so ordinary that few people consider how it works. At any moment, more than two dozen satellites orbit roughly twenty thousand kilometres above the Earth, each carrying a precise atomic clock. Each satellite continuously broadcasts its position and the exact time the signal was sent. A receiver on the ground measures how long the signal took to arrive, and from that calculates its distance to the satellite. Signals from at least four satellites allow the receiver to fix its position in three dimensions. Remarkably, the system depends on relativity: without corrections for the way satellite clocks run at different speeds, errors of kilometres would accumulate daily.

retellLecture.title: The invention of air conditioning
retellLecture.sample: The lecture traced the invention of air conditioning. In 1902 Willis Carrier solved a printing problem caused by humid air by blowing air over chilled coils, creating the first modern air conditioner. For decades the technology served factories, theatres, and department stores, with cheap home units arriving in the 1950s. The speaker noted its effects: rapid growth of hot regions, sealed-window building design, and heavy electricity demand during heatwaves.
retellLecture.text: In 1902, a young engineer named Willis Carrier was asked to solve a printing problem: humid air made paper expand and ink misalign. His solution — blowing air over chilled coils to remove moisture — became the first modern air conditioner. For decades the technology served factories, theatres, and department stores rather than homes, and movie palaces even advertised cooled air to attract summer customers. Cheap units for houses arrived in the 1950s and quickly reshaped daily life. Air conditioning enabled the rapid growth of hot, previously uncomfortable regions, changed building design towards sealed windows, and today accounts for a significant share of electricity demand during heatwaves.

respondToSituation.prompt: Your mobile phone was stolen from your bag on a crowded bus about an hour ago. You have just found the local police station. Go to the counter and report the theft. What would you say?

summarizeGroupDiscussion.topic: Some doctors recommend that secondary schools start later in the morning to suit teenagers' sleep patterns. Discuss.
summarizeGroupDiscussion.sample: The students debated whether secondary schools should start later to match teenagers' sleep patterns. Speaker A supported the change, citing research on teenage body clocks and improved attendance in schools that delayed lessons. Speaker B objected that transport, timetables, and after-school commitments make a later start impractical. Speaker C proposed a one-term trial for a single year group with proper evaluation. They agreed to support a carefully planned trial rather than an immediate school-wide change.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: I think the science is clear. Teenagers' body clocks genuinely run later than adults', so making them start lessons at eight means most of the class is half asleep. Schools that moved to a nine o'clock start report better attendance and better grades.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The biology might be right, but the timetable isn't. Buses, teachers' schedules, and after-school clubs are all built around the current times. A later start would push everything back, and students doing sport or part-time jobs would get home much later.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: Couldn't we test it first? One term, one year group, start at nine and compare attendance, results, and how tired students say they feel. Real data beats arguments.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: That sounds sensible, but a trial needs parents on board too, especially the ones who drop children off before work.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: If it's one year group with proper bus adjustments and clear evaluation, I could support it. I just don't want it imposed overnight on everyone.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: Agreed. And even a small change, like moving the first lesson to a lighter subject, might help while the trial runs.

summarizeGroupDiscussion.topic: A city council is debating whether to close the city zoo and move the animals to open wildlife sanctuaries. Discuss.
summarizeGroupDiscussion.sample: The students discussed whether the city zoo should close and its animals be relocated to sanctuaries. Speaker A argued that enclosures cannot meet modern welfare standards, while Speaker B defended the zoo's conservation funding and breeding programmes. Speaker C highlighted the educational value of seeing animals first-hand. They concluded that the decision should depend on welfare and conservation standards, with relocation judged case by case.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: I believe the zoo has had its day. Modern animal welfare standards show that even well-designed enclosures are tiny compared with natural ranges, and sanctuaries give animals far better lives.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: I partly agree, but zoos do real work. This one funds field conservation projects and runs breeding programmes for endangered species — species that might already be extinct without them.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: There's also education. Most people will never see an elephant in the wild; a good zoo visit is what makes children care about conservation in the first place.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Fair points, but documentaries and sanctuaries with webcams can teach the same lessons without keeping animals in enclosures. And sanctuaries still allow some public access.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Then the real question is the standard, not the existence. If the zoo meets modern welfare and conservation standards, keep it and invest in improvements; if it can't, relocate the animals.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: I'd add a practical point: relocation itself is risky and expensive for older animals. Any move should be judged case by case, species by species.

summarizeWrittenText.passage: For centuries, lighthouses were the difference between safe arrival and disaster for ships approaching dangerous coastlines. Early towers burned wood or coal, and their keepers endured long periods of isolation to maintain the light through the night. The nineteenth century brought revolutionary changes: lenses that concentrated light into powerful beams, and eventually electric lamps that could be seen from more than thirty kilometres away. Yet technology did not make keepers redundant immediately, since lamps still required constant cleaning and winding. Automation finally arrived in the twentieth century, and today many lighthouses operate unattended, monitored remotely. Ironically, decommissioned lighthouses now attract tourists, historians, and photographers who celebrate the romantic era of the men who kept the lights burning.
summarizeWrittenText.sample: Lighthouses protected ships from dangerous coastlines for centuries, progressing from wood fires to powerful electric beams; although automation eventually removed the need for resident keepers, decommissioned lighthouses now attract visitors who commemorate the isolated keepers of the pre-automated era.

summarizeWrittenText.passage: Psychologists increasingly describe habits as automatic responses to familiar situations rather than conscious decisions. When a behaviour is repeated in the same context — coffee after waking, a walk after lunch — control gradually shifts from deliberate thought to automatic cues, which explains why habits feel effortless but also resist change. Research suggests that successful habit formation depends less on motivation than on context: attaching a new behaviour to an existing routine, and making the desired action obvious and convenient, dramatically improves results. Conversely, breaking a habit rarely succeeds through willpower alone; altering the environment, so that the old cue no longer triggers the response, proves far more effective. This view reframes self-improvement as a matter of designing surroundings rather than summoning determination.
summarizeWrittenText.sample: Habits are automatic responses to contextual cues rather than decisions; research shows that forming them depends on attaching new behaviours to existing routines and convenient environments, while breaking them works better through changing surroundings than willpower.

summarizeSpokenText.title: The psychology of first impressions
summarizeSpokenText.sample: The speaker explained that we form impressions of strangers within a fraction of a second, based heavily on facial cues such as trustworthiness and competence. These first impressions act as an anchor, so later information is filtered through them and a bad first impression takes far more evidence to change than a good one. However, the speaker stressed that impressions can be revised, especially when people have strong motives to cooperate, and that time together provides more reliable information.
summarizeSpokenText.audio: When we meet someone for the first time, we form an impression within a fraction of a second — long before any meaningful exchange of information. Research shows that these snap judgements rely heavily on the face: cues such as trustworthiness and competence are read from facial structure and expression almost instantly. First impressions then act as an anchor; later information is filtered through them, so changing a bad first impression takes far more evidence than confirming a good one. Yet they are not destiny. Impressions can be revised, particularly when we have strong motives to cooperate, and time together gives more reliable information about a person's actual behaviour.

summarizeSpokenText.title: The Hanseatic League
summarizeSpokenText.sample: The lecture described the Hanseatic League, an alliance of merchant towns led by Lübeck that dominated northern European trade from the twelfth to the seventeenth century. Members traded salt, herring, grain, timber, and cloth through a network stretching from London to Novgorod, maintaining trading posts abroad, their own ships, and even the ability to wage war. The league declined as nation-states grew stronger and trade shifted towards the Atlantic, but for three centuries it made northern commerce organised and secure.
summarizeSpokenText.audio: Between the twelfth and seventeenth centuries, the Hanseatic League dominated trade across northern Europe. It was not a state but a loose alliance of merchant towns, led by Lübeck, that cooperated to protect shipping and secure trading privileges. Members traded salt, herring, grain, timber, and cloth through a network stretching from London to Novgorod, and they established trading posts, known as kontors, in foreign cities. The league maintained its own ships and even waged war when necessary. Its decline came as nation-states grew stronger and trade routes shifted towards the Atlantic, yet for three centuries it made northern commerce remarkably organised and secure.
